claims.assertion: The trip is metered (RydeTAXI), so extra distance adds directly to the fare: GPS records 20.1 km actual against a 15.5 km optimal route (+4.6 km, +30%) and the fare confirms 20.08 km was billed (F1, F6).
One off-route segment ran 12:46–13:07, covering 9.70 km where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, i.e. +4.08 km of unchallenged detour (F3).

No rider consent exists for that segment: the chat record contains no in-app messages at all before the segment started, and F8 is a driver statement made after the trip, which is a claim and not consent (F7, F8).

The driver's only explanation is that his GPS routed him off at Paya Lebar; the policy excuses a reroute only where an LTA DataMall traffic incident on the replaced optimal stretch is on record, and no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window (F8, F12).

Congestion does not excuse the segment: the expressways used were flowing at 60–69 km/h bands (F9, F10), and Paya Lebar Road at 30–39 km/h (F11) is route evidence only and cannot alone exempt a segment under RD-4(b) (F9, F10, F11, F12).
The refund is computable from the fare: the excess distance billed is $6.50 (4.61 km × $1.4099/km), which is the amount overcharged for the unexcused segment under RD-2's metered branch (F4, F1, F3).

Because RD-2 refund is greater than zero, RD-1 is breached, and the driver's 90-day record shows 3 upheld route disputes already, so the case is a repeated route violation and warrants account review (F15, F4).

weaknesses: The rider's own side is thin on evidence: there is no rider message at all (F7), so we have no statement, ETA screenshot or pick-up complaint timestamp to corroborate the version in the complaint; the judge may note the complaint itself is sworn only by the rider.

F12 records no incidents, but the driver may argue F11 (Paya Lebar Road, band 4, 30–39 km/h) plus his GPS statement F8 amounts to a reasonable reroute; although RD-4(b) says a band alone cannot exempt a segment, the judge could read the combination more generously.

The extra 4.6 km in F1 does not map one-for-one onto the 4.08 km segment in F3 — roughly 0.5 km of routing noise/matching jitter inside the 200 m corridor is not attributable to the segment, and RD-2 expressly refuses that residual, so the refund is capped at $6.50 (F4).
Rider profile shows 1 dispute in 90 d, 0 upheld (F14), which the driver can use to suggest a low success history, though RD-6's flag threshold concerns the driver's record, not the rider's.

claims.assertion: The record shows one off-route segment only: 12:46–13:07, 9.70 km driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km (F3). The driver's account is that the GPS directed him off at Paya Lebar (F8), and the traffic record for that window is consistent with congestion on the plotted route rather than with a road closure or incident (F9, F10, F11, F12).

Because the trip is metered, only the unexempted segment's extra kilometres can support any refund, and the fare record quantifies that distance at $6.50 (4.61 km × $1.4099/km) against a total charge of $42.52 (F4, F6) — so the whole of the rider's complaint cannot be refunded even if the segment is not exempted.

The rider's complaint that 'he never asked me' is confirmed by the record: there are no in-app chat messages at all, so no rider message before 12:46 agrees to the route taken (F7). The driver therefore has no rider consent, general or specific, to rely on for the segment under RD-5.

claims.assertion: The driver's written statement that he 'followed my GPS' (F8) is not a rider message and cannot be consent: only the rider's own message sent before the segment counts, and the chatbot/statement record shows none (F7, F8).

Even so, the segment is not a driver errand and shows no stop: it is a continuous loop of 9.70 km from 12:46 to 13:07 with no stationary period away from the pickup or drop-off (F3), i.e. a route choice, not a detour to serve the driver's own business.

The traffic record shows the alternative corridor (Paya Lebar Road, 30–39 km/h, band 4) was slow while the expressways were free-flowing at 60–69 km/h, and no incident was recorded anywhere near the route (F9, F11, F12); the record therefore does not supply the 'reasonable cause' that RD-4 requires for the replaced optimal segment.

Profile facts cut against us on RD-6: the driver has 5 disputes and 3 upheld (route: 3) in 90 days (F15), so if any segment is held non-exempt the judge may add the repeated-route-deviation flag even though we argue the segment itself is the only issue.

events.body:
→ D1: The opponent's own facts defeat the excuse: RD-4 requires traffic evidence about the replaced optimal segment, yet F12 records no incident near the route and F9/F10 show the expressways used running at 60–69 km/h bands, so the Paya Lebar exit (F8) is unexplained; the segment remains an unexempted detour of +4.08 km (F3). [F3 F8 F9 F10 F12] [RD-1 RD-4]
→ D2 (concedes): Conceded as to scope: we never asked for the whole $42.52 — the claim is the $6.50 excess-distance component in F4, which is exactly the RD-2 metered calculation (4.61 km × $1.4099/km) applied to the unexempted segment. [F4 F6 F3] [RD-2 FARE-1]
→ D4: The opponent concedes the central point: there is no rider message before the 12:46 segment start (F7) and the driver's post-trip statement (F8) is a claim, not consent, so the segment is not saved by RD-5. [F7 F8] [RD-5]
→ D5: We do not allege a driver errand or a stop; whether the segment is a continuous loop matters not, because RD-1 requires the driver to take the shortest and most direct route absent reasonable cause, and neither a loop nor 'my GPS said so' (F8) is such a cause with no incident on record (F12). [F3 F8 F12] [RD-1 RD-2]
→ D6: Agreed, and this is dispositive against the driver: F12 shows no incident near the route, so RD-4(a) is unsatisfied, and F11's band 4 cannot exempt a segment on its own under RD-4(b) — the segment therefore falls to RD-2. [F11 F12] [RD-4 RD-2]
→ D7 (concedes): We raise no safety allegation, so SAFE-1/SAFE-2 are not engaged; the case is purely a fare/distance dispute on F1–F6. [F7 F8] [SAFE-1 SAFE-2]
→ D8: The service history the opponent cites is itself the flag basis: F15 records 5 disputes, 3 upheld and specifically 3 route deviations in 90 days, which is the 'repeated' pattern RD-6 targets once the RD-2 refund here exceeds zero; the 640 trips and 4.5 rating do not negate a metered overcharge proven on GPS and fare records (F4, F6). [F15 F4 F6 F3] [RD-6 RD-2]
Revised ask: refund_partial $6.50

points.response: The opponent's own facts defeat the excuse: RD-4 requires traffic evidence about the replaced optimal segment, yet F12 records no incident near the route and F9/F10 show the expressways used running at 60–69 km/h bands, so the Paya Lebar exit (F8) is unexplained; the segment remains an unexempted detour of +4.08 km (F3).

Conceded as to scope: we never asked for the whole $42.52 — the claim is the $6.50 excess-distance component in F4, which is exactly the RD-2 metered calculation (4.61 km × $1.4099/km) applied to the unexempted segment.

The opponent concedes the central point: there is no rider message before the 12:46 segment start (F7) and the driver's post-trip statement (F8) is a claim, not consent, so the segment is not saved by RD-5.

Agreed, and this is dispositive against the driver: F12 shows no incident near the route, so RD-4(a) is unsatisfied, and F11's band 4 cannot exempt a segment on its own under RD-4(b) — the segment therefore falls to RD-2.

? RD-5 rider agreed to this route before the detour; scope of that agreement [F3] RULE: exempt only if a RIDER message sent before 12:46:55 agrees AND the agreement covers this segment. The driver's only explanation is that his GPS routed him off at Paya Lebar; the policy excuses a reroute only where an LTA DataMall traffic incident on the replaced optimal stretch is on record, and no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window (F8, F12).

Congestion does not excuse the segment: the expressways used were flowing at 60–69 km/h bands (F9, F10), and Paya Lebar Road at 30–39 km/h (F11) is route evidence only and cannot alone exempt a segment under RD-4(b) (F9, F10, F11, F12).
The refund is computable from the fare: the excess distance billed is $6.50 (4.61 km × $1.4099/km), which is the amount overcharged for the unexcused segment under RD-2's metered branch (F4, F1, F3).

Because RD-2 refund is greater than zero, RD-1 is breached, and the driver's 90-day record shows 3 upheld route disputes already, so the case is a repeated route violation and warrants account review (F15, F4).

weaknesses: The rider's own side is thin on evidence: there is no rider message at all (F7), so we have no statement, ETA screenshot or pick-up complaint timestamp to corroborate the version in the complaint; the judge may note the complaint itself is sworn only by the rider.

F12 records no incidents, but the driver may argue F11 (Paya Lebar Road, band 4, 30–39 km/h) plus his GPS statement F8 amounts to a reasonable reroute; although RD-4(b) says a band alone cannot exempt a segment, the judge could read the combination more generously.

The extra 4.6 km in F1 does not map one-for-one onto the 4.08 km segment in F3 — roughly 0.5 km of routing noise/matching jitter inside the 200 m corridor is not attributable to the segment, and RD-2 expressly refuses that residual, so the refund is capped at $6.50 (F4).
Rider profile shows 1 dispute in 90 d, 0 upheld (F14), which the driver can use to suggest a low success history, though RD-6's flag threshold concerns the driver's record, not the rider's.

claims.assertion: The record shows one off-route segment only: 12:46–13:07, 9.70 km driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km (F3). The driver's account is that the GPS directed him off at Paya Lebar (F8), and the traffic record for that window is consistent with congestion on the plotted route rather than with a road closure or incident (F9, F10, F11, F12).

Because the trip is metered, only the unexempted segment's extra kilometres can support any refund, and the fare record quantifies that distance at $6.50 (4.61 km × $1.4099/km) against a total charge of $42.52 (F4, F6) — so the whole of the rider's complaint cannot be refunded even if the segment is not exempted.

The rider's complaint that 'he never asked me' is confirmed by the record: there are no in-app chat messages at all, so no rider message before 12:46 agrees to the route taken (F7). The driver therefore has no rider consent, general or specific, to rely on for the segment under RD-5.
claims.void_reason: citation check: cites G11 — not a citable clause

claims.assertion: The driver's written statement that he 'followed my GPS' (F8) is not a rider message and cannot be consent: only the rider's own message sent before the segment counts, and the chatbot/statement record shows none (F7, F8).

Even so, the segment is not a driver errand and shows no stop: it is a continuous loop of 9.70 km from 12:46 to 13:07 with no stationary period away from the pickup or drop-off (F3), i.e. a route choice, not a detour to serve the driver's own business.

The traffic record shows the alternative corridor (Paya Lebar Road, 30–39 km/h, band 4) was slow while the expressways were free-flowing at 60–69 km/h, and no incident was recorded anywhere near the route (F9, F11, F12); the record therefore does not supply the 'reasonable cause' that RD-4 requires for the replaced optimal segment.

No rider or driver message, and no complaint statement, contains a threat, intimidation, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation; the rider's complaint is limited to the distance and the fare, so SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation is not engaged.

The driver's own service history is strong — 980 days on the platform, 4.5 rating, 640 trips in 90 days (F15) — and the GPS shows the car stopped nowhere it was not asked to go, so there is no basis for flagging the account on this record; the profile facts are offered only against that request, not to decide the segment (F14, F15).

weaknesses: No consent exists in any form: F7 records zero in-app chat messages, so the rider never sent a message before the 12:46 segment start, and the driver's post-trip statement (F8) cannot supply it under RD-5/G11.
The scale is hard to defend: the off-route segment added 4.08 km on a 15.5 km optimal route, +30% overall and +12.2 min (F1, F2, F3), and the fare record confirms the excess was billed at $6.50 (F4).

The driver's own explanation — following the GPS off at Paya Lebar (F8) — is not a RD-4 excuse: traffic facts show no incident near the route (F12) and only moderate speed bands (F9, F10, F11), and RD-4 requires the traffic evidence to be about the replaced optimal segment, which it is not.

Profile facts cut against us on RD-6: the driver has 5 disputes and 3 upheld (route: 3) in 90 days (F15), so if any segment is held non-exempt the judge may add the repeated-route-deviation flag even though we argue the segment itself is the only issue.

points.response: The opponent's own facts defeat the excuse: RD-4 requires traffic evidence about the replaced optimal segment, yet F12 records no incident near the route and F9/F10 show the expressways used running at 60–69 km/h bands, so the Paya Lebar exit (F8) is unexplained; the segment remains an unexempted detour of +4.08 km (F3).

Conceded as to scope: we never asked for the whole $42.52 — the claim is the $6.50 excess-distance component in F4, which is exactly the RD-2 metered calculation (4.61 km × $1.4099/km) applied to the unexempted segment.

The opponent concedes the central point: there is no rider message before the 12:46 segment start (F7) and the driver's post-trip statement (F8) is a claim, not consent, so the segment is not saved by RD-5.

We do not allege a driver errand or a stop; whether the segment is a continuous loop matters not, because RD-1 requires the driver to take the shortest and most direct route absent reasonable cause, and neither a loop nor 'my GPS said so' (F8) is such a cause with no incident on record (F12).

Agreed, and this is dispositive against the driver: F12 shows no incident near the route, so RD-4(a) is unsatisfied, and F11's band 4 cannot exempt a segment on its own under RD-4(b) — the segment therefore falls to RD-2.
We raise no safety allegation, so SAFE-1/SAFE-2 are not engaged; the case is purely a fare/distance dispute on F1–F6.

The service history the opponent cites is itself the flag basis: F15 records 5 disputes, 3 upheld and specifically 3 route deviations in 90 days, which is the 'repeated' pattern RD-6 targets once the RD-2 refund here exceeds zero; the 640 trips and 4.5 rating do not negate a metered overcharge proven on GPS and fare records (F4, F6).

Concede the mechanism: the trip is metered and the meter recorded 20.08 km billed in a $42.52 total (F6), so extra kilometres do reach the fare — but F1 shows the total excess is 4.6 km while only 4.08 km is attributed to the single segment (F3, F1), which is exactly why the correct figure under RD-2 is not the whole difference.

Conceded: F3 is the only off-route segment on the record, 9.70 km driven against 5.62 km optimal for +4.08 km, and the driver's statement that he followed his GPS off at Paya Lebar (F8) does not explain that distance.

Conceded, and this is the honest weak point of the driver's case: F7 records no in-app messages at all, so nothing the rider sent precedes the 12:46 segment start, and the driver's post-trip statement (F8) is a claim, not consent, under RD-5 and G11.

Conceded on the absence of an RD-4 excuse: F12 records no traffic incident near the route in the trip window, and RD-4 requires a DataMall incident on the replaced optimal stretch ('reasonable cause'), which the driver's GPS statement (F8) cannot substitute for.

Agreed and it does not help either side: the expressways were flowing at 60–69 km/h (F9, F10) while Paya Lebar Road ran at 30–39 km/h band 4 (F11), and RD-4(b) says a band alone cannot exempt a segment, so the traffic record neither excuses the segment nor makes it a reasonable-cause reroute.

Mostly conceded as to quantum: F4 gives the billed excess distance as $6.50 (4.61 km × $1.4099/km derived from this trip's own distance fare), which is the RD-2 metered measure and is computable from the fare record; the driver does not dispute that figure.

Conceded in part: since F4 is above zero the segment is unexempted under RD-2, and F15 shows 3 upheld route disputes in 90 days, so on this record the RD-6 flag condition is met; the driver asks only that the flag be noted as reflecting a single 4.08 km routing lapse against 640 trips in 90 days (F15), not a finding of bad faith.

notices.text: We reviewed your trip and are refunding part of your fare. The driver took an off-route detour: on a stretch of the trip he drove 9.70 km where the best route is 5.62 km, an extra 4.08 km. Nothing on record exempts that stretch — there was no traffic incident and you did not agree to the change. We are sending you a $5.75 Ryde voucher for the extra distance. No action is needed from you. Thanks for flagging it.
